title: Observation-based data-gathering method for cultural ecosystem services in urban green spaces
author: Valença Pinto, Inácio, et al.
materials: The method is centred on a mobile app developed on the AppSheet platform (appsheet.com). The app allows the observer to record geolocated information on observed activities (see Table 1 for a complete list of options), time-related information (season, week period, and timeslot), weather-related information (rain conditions, temperature, cloud coverage, solar exposure, wind speed) and user characteristics (age group, biological sex, individual vs group, number of users, groups with children). It also identifies and characterises recreational equipment in each UGS (e.g., benches, water fountains, waste bins, and different sports and cultural equipment types). All this was implemented in a single app, allowing for the centralisation and pre-treatment of the information, reducing posterior data preparation time. The weather variables are measured using adequate equipment, i.e., via a handheld digital anemometer and a handheld digital thermometer. We identified and recorded 33 activities based on the observed behaviour of park users, and we included an option for “Doing other activities in nature” to account for any other relevant uses not included in the established list. All data recorded in the app was geolocated over high-resolution aerial imagery to ensure spatial accuracy. The mobile app was designed to ensure consistency and efficiency in data collection. No records were saved if any data was missing. The number of users recorded depended on whether the user was an individual or part of a group. Gender options were tailored to each user type, with a “Mixed” option only available for groups. The list of available activity options in the app was restricted based on the user's motion status (in motion vs stationary), ensuring that only relevant activities were recorded. Before going to the study areas, prepare all the equipment, check battery levels, and pack a power bank for extra charges. Arrive at the site at least 15 min before the official start of data collection. Turn on all devices that might need a starting time to adjust to local conditions, e.g., activate the GPS of the mobile device and let the thermometer adjust to external conditions.

steps.title: Prepare equipment and devices
steps.instruction: Before fieldwork, gather all required equipment, verify battery levels, and pack a power bank for extra charging. Arrive at the study site at least 15 minutes before the scheduled start. Power on all devices that need a warm‑up period, activate the mobile device GPS, and allow the handheld digital thermometer to equilibrate to ambient conditions.

substeps.instruction: Check battery levels of mobile device, anemometer, and thermometer.
Pack a fully charged power bank.
Travel to the site and arrive ≥15 min early.
Turn on the mobile phone, GPS, anemometer, and thermometer.
Let the thermometer adjust to external temperature.

steps.title: Configure and launch data collection app
steps.instruction: Install the custom AppSheet application, set up its fields as described in Table 1, and enable geolocation over high‑resolution aerial imagery. Load the list of 33 activity options (including “Doing other activities in nature”) and the user‑characteristic fields (age group, biological sex, individual vs group, number of users, groups with children). Ensure the app enforces the rule that no record is saved if any field is missing and that activity options are filtered by motion status (in motion vs stationary).

substeps.instruction: Open the AppSheet app on the mobile device.
Verify field definitions (Field ID, description, visibility, dependence, value type, default) match Table 1.
Confirm the activity list contains 33 options and the “other” catch‑all.
Activate geolocation and link to high‑resolution aerial maps.
Check that the app blocks incomplete entries.

steps.title: Record user observations in the field
steps.instruction: While at the urban green space, observe each park user or group, select the appropriate activity, and fill in all user‑characteristic fields. Use the handheld digital anemometer to record wind speed and the handheld digital thermometer for temperature. The app will automatically capture the GPS coordinates. Distinguish between individual observations (single user) and group observations (two or more users sharing an experience). Save each record only when all required data are entered.

substeps.instruction: Identify whether the observed user is individual or part of a group.
Select the observed activity from the 33‑option list.
Enter user characteristics: age group, biological sex, individual vs group, number of users, presence of children.
Measure wind speed with the digital anemometer (m s⁻¹).
Measure ambient temperature with the digital thermometer (°C).
Confirm GPS location is recorded.
Submit the record; the app will reject if any field is missing.

steps.title: Convert weather measurements for analysis
steps.instruction: After data collection, transform raw weather values: convert wind‑speed measurements (m s⁻¹) to Beaufort classes using the provided ranges, and map temperature readings (°C) to comfort zones.

substeps.instruction: Wind‑speed → Beaufort class: 0.28 m s⁻¹ = Calm (0), 1.39 m s⁻¹ = Light Air (1), 3.06 m s⁻¹ = Light Breeze (2), 5.28 m s⁻¹ = Gentle Breeze (3), 7.78 m s⁻¹ = Moderate Breeze (4), 10.56 m s⁻¹ = Fresh Breeze (5), 13.61 m s⁻¹ = Strong Breeze (6), 16.94 m s⁻¹ = Near Gale (7).

Temperature → comfort zone: ≤0 °C = Sub‑zero (negative), 0–16 °C = Uncomfortable (too cold), 16–22 °C = Slightly uncomfortable (cold), 22–29 °C = Comfortable, 29–37 °C = Slightly uncomfortable (hot), ≥45 °C = Uncomfortable (too hot).

steps.title: Group observed activities for analysis
steps.instruction: Assign each of the 33 recorded activities to one of eight analytical categories to simplify downstream statistical work.

steps.title: Perform spatial heat‑map and autocorrelation analyses
steps.instruction: Use the geolocated observation dataset to generate spatial visualisations and test spatial relationships.

substeps.instruction: Apply Kernel Density Estimation to produce heat‑maps of observation density for each urban green space.
Compute Global Moran's I to assess spatial autocorrelation between locations of stationary activity groups and the positions of recreational equipment (e.g., benches, fountains, sports gear).
